nameStory: This jelly fungus gets its name from its bright orange color and distinctive spot-like appearance on decaying wood. The alternative name "orange witch's butter" comes from folklore — people once thought these mysterious, gelatinous blobs that appeared overnight on logs were supernatural butter left by witches.
description: Orange Jelly Spot is a small, gelatinous fungus that looks like drops of bright orange jelly scattered on rotting wood. These squishy, translucent blobs are usually less than an inch across and have a smooth, glossy surface that glistens when wet. Unlike mushrooms with caps and stems, this fungus forms irregular, cushion-like masses that can merge together. It belongs to a group called jelly fungi because of its distinctive rubbery, bouncy texture.

idTips.label: Jelly-like texture
idTips.description: Feels like firm gelatin or a rubber bouncy ball when poked — it springs back and doesn't crumble like other fungi

idTips.label: Bright orange color
idTips.description: Vibrant orange to yellow-orange, becoming more translucent and glassy when wet, duller when dry

idTips.label: Spot-like shape
idTips.description: Forms irregular blobs, cushions, or brain-like folds, usually under an inch wide, often clustered together

idTips.label: Smooth, glossy surface
idTips.description: Surface is shiny and wet-looking, like it's been covered in clear nail polish

idTips.label: Growing on dead wood
idTips.description: Always found on decaying logs, branches, or stumps — never on living trees or soil

idTips.label: No mushroom structure
idTips.description: Lacks the typical cap, stem, or gills of mushrooms — just amorphous jelly-like masses

habitat: Look for Orange Jelly Spot on decaying hardwood logs, fallen branches, and old stumps throughout New England's forests. It particularly favors oak, maple, and birch wood that's been rotting for at least a year or two. You'll find it in both deep woods and forest edges, from sea level to mountain elevations.

seasonality.spring: Fresh orange blobs begin appearing on logs as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture. This is prime time for bright, plump specimens.
seasonality.summer: Continues fruiting during humid periods, though may shrivel and become less noticeable during dry spells. Look after summer rainstorms for renewed growth.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for Orange Jelly Spot as autumn moisture returns. Cool, damp conditions create ideal growing weather and specimens are most abundant.
seasonality.winter: Persists through mild winter periods, becoming darker and more shriveled in cold weather. May appear dried and crusty but will plump up again with moisture.

funFact: Orange Jelly Spot can completely dry up into a hard, crusty film during drought, looking almost dead, then magically plump back up into its full jelly-like glory within hours of the next rainstorm — like a natural sponge coming back to life!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other orange jelly fungi, but Orange Jelly Spot forms simple cushion-like blobs while Fan-shaped Jelly Fungus grows in distinctive fan or spoon shapes. Remember: "spots are simple, fans are fancy."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "orange witch's butter," this fungus is completely unrelated to the more common "witch's butter" (Tremella mesenterica), which is yellow and belongs to a different family entirely. The shared nickname creates confusion among foragers.
compareHints: Orange Jelly Spot forms simple, rounded cushions while its relative Fan-shaped Jelly Fungus grows in distinctive spoon or fan shapes with flattened tops. Yellow Hat Jelly creates tiny cup-like structures on thin stalks, quite different from the blob-like Orange Jelly Spot. All three share the same bouncy, gelatinous texture but have very different growth forms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Fan-shaped Jelly Fungus stands out from its relatives Orange Jelly Spot and Yellow Hat Jelly by its distinctive flattened, spoon-like shape.
